_comment: ORM fields and column mapping -- feature 18. Two owner decisions
(OWNER-DECISIONS.md Batch 3 FIELD-DEC-01 + Batch 5 FIELD-DEC-02):
FIELD-DEC-01 (owner overrode the Python-master default): reconcile the field
model BEHAVIOUR-BY-BEHAVIOUR (ADR-0004 best-implementation-prevails), NOT a
single language as master. The DECLARATION SURFACE stays each language's
idiom -- Python field OBJECTS (IntegerField(...)), PHP reflection on typed
properties, Ruby DSL class-methods (integer_field), Node declarative
FieldDefinition objects -- and only the BEHAVIOUR on top is reconciled. The
one gap FIELD-DEC-01 names is closed here: callable defaults now work in ALL
FOUR (PHP was the hold-out).
FIELD-DEC-02 (fixes): DELETE the Python cross-engine DDL MOCK
(test_orm_v3_13_11::test_engine_dispatch monkeypatched execute/
get_database_type and asserted a SQL STRING) and replace it with a
REAL-engine DDL test; fix the Ruby decimal precision (decimal_field emitted
REAL, dropping the declared scale); anchor the PHP datetime NAME heuristic;
fix the Ruby FK auto related_name.
The five reconciled behaviours proven here, NO MOCKS -- every case drives a
REAL database (SQLite for the type/JSON/default/decimal-DDL cases, and REAL
PostgreSQL/MySQL/MSSQL/Firebird for the engine-DDL cases):
1. PHP CALLABLE DEFAULTS (FIELD-CALLABLE-DEFAULT-PHP): a PHP typed property
cannot hold a Closure default, so the idiomatic channel is a
fieldDefaults() method hook -- resolved PER INSTANCE on construct,
DROPPED from the DDL. Python (_resolve_default), Ruby (per-instance
lambda) and Node (typeof===function) already did this; the four-way
'callable default' cases prove all four now agree.
2. DECIMAL(p,s) PARITY (FIELD-DECIMAL-PRECISION): a decimal field produces
a real DECIMAL(precision, scale) column, identical on
PG/MySQL/MSSQL/Firebird/SQLite. Ruby's decimal_field was emitting REAL
and silently dropping precision/scale (the named bug); MEASURED, none of
the four had a decimal->DECIMAL(p,s) path, so each got its idiomatic one:
Ruby fixes decimal_field's type_map; Python adds DecimalField(precision,
scale); Node adds type:'decimal' + precision/scale to FieldDefinition;
PHP adds a $decimals overlay ([prop => [p, s]], the same array-property
idiom as $foreignKeys, because a PHP float property cannot carry a
precision/scale). FloatField/NumericField stay REAL (documented float
default -- for exact money store minor units in an integer).
3. REAL-ENGINE DDL, NOT A MOCK (FIELD-ENGINE-DDL-MOCK -> REAL): create the
table on the REAL engine and read the column type back from the engine's
OWN catalog (information_schema for PG/MySQL/MSSQL, RDB$ for Firebird).
BOOLEAN -> PG boolean / MySQL tinyint(1) / MSSQL bit / Firebird INTEGER;
JSON -> PG jsonb / MySQL json / MSSQL nvarchar(max) / Firebird BLOB
SUB_TYPE TEXT; DECIMAL(12,4) -> precision 12 scale 4 (Firebird scale -4,
a scaled INT64). The real test caught a divergence the mock could not:
Node mapped a Firebird boolean to SMALLINT while Python/PHP/Ruby (and the
documented contract) map it to INTEGER -- Node is aligned to INTEGER.
4. PHP DATETIME HEURISTIC ANCHOR (FIELD-PHP-DATETIME-HEURISTIC, PHP-only):
the /(_at$|date|time)/i SUBSTRING match wrongly inferred 'datetime' for
updated_by (has 'date' in up-date-d), runtime and downtime (end in
'time'). Anchored to /(_at$)|((?:^|_)(?:date|time|datetime|timestamp)$)/i
-- a whole trailing segment -- so created_at, updated_at, a *_date and a
*_time column still resolve while the substrings do not. This is a
PHP-only behaviour: Python/Ruby/Node declare the type explicitly, they do
not infer it from a name.
5. RUBY FK RELATED-NAME (FIELD-FK-RELATEDNAME-RUBY, Ruby-only):
foreign_key_field's auto related_name used a naive downcase + 's'
(Category -> 'categorys'); it now routes through a new Tina4.pluralize
that mirrors the existing Tina4.singularize (Category -> 'categories').
This is scoped Ruby-only per the owner call; MEASURED, Python/PHP/Node
still derive the FK has-many name as declaring-class-lowercased + 's'
(a latent cross-language parity gap, flagged for a follow-up, not widened
here).
NOT converged: the DECLARATION SURFACE. Each language keeps its idiom.
Each invariant names a REAL suite file per framework carrying the SAME case
names in each language's own idiom, which scripts/audit-contract-fixtures.py
normalises and matches. The two PHP-only / Ruby-only invariants name only the
framework whose declaration model has that behaviour.
feature: 18 - ORM fields and column mapping (FIELD-DEC-01 reconcile behaviour-by-behaviour + PHP callable defaults; FIELD-DEC-02 real-engine DDL replacing the mock, Ruby DECIMAL(p,s), PHP datetime anchor, Ruby FK name)

invariants.rule: Each declared field type round-trips through a REAL database (write coercion -> DDL column -> read hydration): a JSON field serializes on write and parses back to a NATIVE object on read; a CALLABLE default is resolved PER INSTANCE (per-row values differ) and is NOT present in the CREATE TABLE DDL (now including PHP, via fieldDefaults()); and a value a JSON field cannot serialize makes save() return FALSE and log the cause (never raise, never silently persist). Identical in all four (Python field objects, PHP reflection, Ruby DSL, Node FieldDefinition).
invariants.why: This pins the reconciled field-model behaviour on top of the four DIVERGENT declaration surfaces (FIELD-DEC-01, kept idiomatic per language). Callable defaults were the one parity gap the audit named -- Python/Ruby/Node resolved a callable default per-instance and dropped it from DDL, PHP could not (a PHP property default cannot be a Closure); PHP now provides them through a fieldDefaults() method hook, so all four agree. The non-serializable-JSON negative pins the fail-loud contract; MEASURED, Python actually RAISED out of save() (its to_db serialization ran outside the transaction try) and was fixed to return False + log like PHP/Ruby/Node. Proven against a REAL SQLite database with real rows and real ORM writes -- no mocks.
cases: each declared field type round trips through a real database
a json field round trips to a native object
a callable default is resolved per instance
a callable default is not present in the create table ddl
a non serializable json value makes save return false and is logged

invariants.rule: A decimal field produces a real DECIMAL(precision, scale) column in the generated DDL, in all four frameworks -- via Ruby decimal_field precision:/scale:, Python DecimalField(precision, scale), Node { type: 'decimal', precision, scale }, and PHP a $decimals overlay. FloatField/NumericField (and their per-language equivalents) stay a floating REAL column.
invariants.why: FIELD-DECIMAL-PRECISION: Ruby's decimal_field STORED precision/scale but emitted REAL, silently dropping the declared scale -- the named bug. MEASURED, none of the four actually emitted DECIMAL(p,s), so each gained an idiomatic decimal declaration that does. The DDL column type is the fix; the in-memory value stays a float (the documented money guidance -- for exact arithmetic store minor units in an integer). Proven against a REAL SQLite database (the declared DECIMAL(12,4) is read back from the created table); the per-engine DECIMAL(p,s) precision/scale is proven on real engines by ormfields-engine-ddl. No mocks.
cases: a decimal field produces a decimal precision scale column

invariants.rule: The engine-specific DDL column types are created on the REAL engine and read back from the engine's OWN catalog match: a BOOLEAN column is PG boolean / MySQL tinyint(1) / MSSQL bit / Firebird INTEGER; a JSON column is PG jsonb / MySQL json / MSSQL nvarchar(max) / Firebird BLOB SUB_TYPE TEXT; a DECIMAL(12,4) column has precision 12 and scale 4 (Firebird stores it as a scaled INT64, scale -4); and a real row of {bool, json object, decimal, datetime} round-trips through those columns. Proven on real PostgreSQL, MySQL, MSSQL and Firebird in all four frameworks.
invariants.why: FIELD-ENGINE-DDL-MOCK -> REAL: the cross-engine DDL mapping was covered ONLY by a Python MOCK (test_orm_v3_13_11::test_engine_dispatch monkeypatched execute + get_database_type and asserted the SQL STRING) -- a no-mock-rule violation that never proved a real engine accepts the DDL. That mock is DELETED; this creates the table on the REAL engine and reads the column type from information_schema (PG/MySQL/MSSQL) or RDB$RELATION_FIELDS/RDB$FIELDS (Firebird). The real test immediately caught a divergence the mock could not: Node emitted SMALLINT for a Firebird boolean while Python/PHP/Ruby emit INTEGER (the documented contract) -- Node is aligned to INTEGER. Gated in require-services (a PG/MySQL/MSSQL skip is a hard failure); Firebird runs when TINA4_TEST_FIREBIRD_URL is set (the lab sets it). No mocks anywhere.
cases: a boolean column is created with the engine native boolean type
a json column is created with the engine native json type
a decimal column is created with decimal precision and scale on the engine
the engine ddl types round trip a real row

invariants.rule: PHP infers a 'datetime' logical column type from a property NAME only via an ANCHORED whole-suffix pattern, so a substring never misfires: updated_by (contains 'date' inside 'up-date-d'), runtime and downtime (end in 'time') are NOT inferred as datetime, while created_at (a _at suffix), a *_date column and a *_time column still ARE. PHP-only: Python, Ruby and Node declare the field type explicitly, they never infer it from a name.
invariants.why: FIELD-PHP-DATETIME-HEURISTIC: the old /(_at$|date|time)/i matched INSIDE a word, so updated_by/runtime/downtime were wrongly typed 'datetime' in the DDL/seeding -- an untested false-positive path. Anchored to /(_at$)|((?:^|_)(?:date|time|datetime|timestamp)$)/i, only reached when the property is not an explicitly \DateTime-typed one (the real type is preferred). This invariant names only the PHP suite because the name heuristic is PHP's alone -- the other three carry the field type on the declaration, so there is no substring to misfire.
cases: updated_by is not inferred as datetime
runtime and downtime are not inferred as datetime
created_at and a date column and a time column are still inferred as datetime

invariants.rule: Ruby's foreign_key_field auto related_name is SMART-pluralized from the DECLARING class name: a Category model declaring a foreign_key_field wires has_many :categories on the referenced model, never the naive :categorys. Ruby-only.
invariants.why: FIELD-FK-RELATEDNAME-RUBY: the auto related_name used a naive downcase + 's' (Category -> 'categorys' -- a broken accessor name), while the hand-written has_many already used smart inflection. It now routes through a new Tina4.pluralize that mirrors Tina4.singularize (y->ies, s/sh/ch/x/z->es, else +s). Scoped Ruby-only per the owner call; this invariant names only the Ruby suite. MEASURED, Python/PHP/Node still derive the FK has-many name as declaring-class-lowercased + 's' -- a latent cross-language parity gap flagged for a follow-up, deliberately not widened in this feature.
cases: a foreign key to Category wires categories not categorys
